note: Both judges saw only the advisory text and the finding text, with opaque ids and an order fixed by a hash unrelated to the arm, and were told the findings come from whole-repository reviews so that most of them being unrelated is expected rather than suspicious. The arm is joined back in afterwards.

judgements.reason: TLS trust/key manager algorithm defaulting to SunX509 instead of PKIX in ConnectionFactoryConfigurator - a certificate-validation weakness, unrelated to ValueReader's unchecked byte-array allocation from a wire-declared length.
Missing permissions: key in GitHub Actions workflows (over-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN). CI supply-chain hardening, not the AMQP frame parser allocation defect.
Absence of SBOM/provenance attestation on the published Maven artifact. A release-metadata gap, no relation to ValueReader.readBytes().
Unpinned GitHub Actions tags and unpinned external checkouts in the release path. Build-integrity issue, not the unchecked allocation in the value decoder.

Property-file TLS path falling through to TrustEverythingTrustManager (MITM). Certificate trust defect in ConnectionFactoryConfigurator, a different file and a different consequence from the OOM allocation.

Unchecked exception from a malformed JSON-RPC body escaping RpcServer.mainloop(), killing the RPC server loop. Different component (RpcServer/JsonRpcServer) and different mechanism (uncaught Throwable), not the ValueReader length-driven allocation.
Certificate and hostname validation defaulting off in the property-based TLS configurator. A trust/authentication defect, unrelated to the wire-declared length allocation in ValueReader.
setNioParams/setSocketConfigurator overwriting the state that carries hostname verification, silently downgrading TLS. Configuration ordering defect in ConnectionFactory, not the parser allocation.
Netty IO layer ignoring the configured hostname verification, permitting broker impersonation. TLS endpoint-identification defect, a different mechanism and consequence from unchecked allocation.

Non-terminating loop in JSONReader.string() on an unterminated string, growing a StringBuilder without bound. Different file (tools/json), different mechanism (CharacterIterator.DONE loop), even though the end state is also OOM; it is not the ValueReader length-declared allocation.
Infinite busy loop in JSONReader.skipWhiteSpace() on an unterminated // comment. JSON tooling hang, not the AMQP ValueReader allocation defect.
Maven wrapper downloading a distribution with no distributionSha256Sum pin. Toolchain supply-chain gap, unrelated to the parser.
Predictable incrementing correlation IDs in RpcClient allowing response forgery on a named reply queue. Different component and a spoofing consequence, not memory exhaustion in ValueReader.

Same file and same untrusted entry point (ValueReader field-table parsing, reachable pre-auth from Connection.Start), but the mechanism is unbounded readTable/readFieldValue/readArray recursion causing StackOverflowError, not the unchecked byte[] allocation from a declared content length; the consequence is a killed connection rather than heap OOM.
LogTrafficListener writing the SASL response (broker password) to logs at TRACE. Credential disclosure through logging, an entirely different defect.

Same file and same line region as P-028 (ValueReader.java:181): missing depth limit on recursive field-table parsing leading to StackOverflowError. Same area as the advisory but a different mechanism (recursion depth, not a wire-declared allocation size) and a different consequence.

frame_max=0 from the broker collapsing the negotiated limit through Math.min and Utils.framePayloadLimit, letting Frame.readFrom allocate up to 2 GB per frame. Different location (AMQConnection.start / Frame / FrameBuilder) and a different mechanism (frame-max negotiation bug), even though it also ends in an oversized allocation; the advisory's defect is inside ValueReader.readBytes.

Exactly the advisory's defect: ValueReader.readBytes() at line 86 allocates new byte[contentLength] from a wire-declared int bounded only by Integer.MAX_VALUE, never against the bytes remaining in the frame, with readFully() only failing afterwards; same pre-authentication reach via readLongstr/type 'x' from the Connection.Start server-properties table, same ~2 GB OOM consequence.

TLS trust/key manager algorithm defaulting to SunX509 instead of PKIX in ConnectionFactoryConfigurator. Certificate-validation weakness on the connection path; nothing to do with Class.forName on a javaReturnType from a system.describe reply in ProcedureDescription.
Missing permissions: key in GitHub Actions workflows, i.e. an over-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN in CI. Supply-chain/CI posture, not the unvalidated reflective class loading in the JSON-RPC tools.
Absence of SBOM and build provenance for the published Maven artifact. A release-metadata gap in pom.xml with no attacker mechanism at all; unrelated to ProcedureDescription's Class.forName.

Unpinned GitHub Actions and unpinned external checkouts (tls-gen, rabbitmq-server) in the release path. Build-time supply-chain risk, a different mechanism, place and consequence from runtime class loading of attacker-supplied class names.

Property-based ssl.enabled defaulting to TrustEverythingTrustManager in ConnectionFactoryConfigurator.setUpSsl. An unauthenticated-TLS/MITM defect in the connection layer, not the JSON-RPC Class.forName issue.

Unchecked exception (NPE from DefaultJsonRpcMapper's unguarded request fields) escaping RpcServer.mainloop, killing the server loop. Touches JSON-RPC code but is a server-side availability defect; the advisory is client-side arbitrary class loading via Class.forName in ProcedureDescription, a different file, mechanism and consequence.

Certificate and hostname validation disabled by default on the property-file TLS path (line 306 / useSslProtocol with TrustEverythingTrustManager). MITM on the AMQP connection, not reflective class loading from a system.describe response.

setNioParams/setSocketConfigurator overwrite the composed socket configurator and silently drop hostname verification in ConnectionFactory. An ordering-dependent TLS downgrade; unrelated to ProcedureDescription.computeReturnTypeAsJavaClass.

The Netty frame handler factory ignores nioParams/socketConf hostname verification and builds the SslHandler from the user SslContext alone. TLS endpoint-identification gap in the IO layer, not the JSON-RPC Class.forName defect.

JSONReader.string() loops forever on an unterminated string because CharacterIterator.DONE never matches the separator, hanging the server and exhausting the heap. Same tools subtree, but a non-terminating-loop DoS in the parser, not unvalidated Class.forName on javaReturnType.

JSONReader.skipWhiteSpace() spins forever on an unterminated // comment. Again a parser busy-loop DoS in com.rabbitmq.tools.json, a different file and mechanism from ProcedureDescription's reflective class loading.
Maven wrapper distribution downloaded with no distributionSha256Sum pin. Build-toolchain integrity issue in .mvn/wrapper, entirely outside the advisory's runtime defect.

Predictable incrementing correlation IDs in RpcClient allow response forgery on a named reply queue. A response-spoofing weakness in the plain RPC client, not class loading from a JSON-RPC service description.
Unbounded recursion in ValueReader.readTable/readFieldValue on nested AMQP field tables causing StackOverflowError. Wire-protocol decoder DoS, a different file, mechanism and consequence.
LogTrafficListener logs the SASL StartOk command at TRACE, leaking broker credentials to application logs. Credential disclosure through logging, unrelated to Class.forName in the JSON-RPC tools.
Same ValueReader depth-limit-free field-table recursion as P-027, reported with the reconnect-loop consequence. AMQP decoder stack exhaustion, not the advisory's reflective class loading defect.

frame_max=0 from the broker collapses the negotiated Math.min and voids maxInboundMessageBodySize, allowing ~2 GB per-frame allocation. Memory-exhaustion defect in AMQConnection/Frame, a different place and consequence.

ValueReader.readBytes allocates a broker-declared length before checking bytes available, enabling a huge pre-auth allocation. Allocation DoS in the AMQP value decoder, not Class.forName on an untrusted javaReturnType.
